lesson.title: Ask for the Moon, Settle for a Favor
lesson.summary: A persuasion strategy that starts with a large, unreasonable request expected to be refused, then follows with a smaller, more reasonable request, which people are more likely to accept than if it had been asked first.
lesson.body:
If the foot-in-the-door technique starts small and builds up, the door-in-the-face technique does the opposite: it starts big, expects to be turned down, and then retreats to the request the persuader wanted all along. Like foot-in-the-door, it is a well studied persuasion tactic, but it works through a different psychological lever, one built around the social discomfort of refusing someone twice.

The classic study is by Robert Cialdini and colleagues in 1975. College students were approached and asked to volunteer as unpaid counselors to juvenile delinquents at a detention facility, a serious commitment of two hours a week for two years. Nearly everyone declined. The same researcher then asked a much smaller favor: would the student be willing to chaperone a single two hour trip to the zoo with a group of juvenile delinquents? Students who had just refused the larger request agreed to the zoo trip at a notably higher rate than students who were simply asked about the zoo trip with no prior request, a difference Cialdini and colleagues described as substantial.

Two explanations are usually offered together. One is the norm of reciprocal concessions: when someone backs off from a large demand to a smaller one, it can feel like they made a concession for your benefit, and social norms push people to reciprocate concessions of their own, in this case by agreeing to the smaller request. The other is perceptual contrast: after hearing an extreme request, a moderate request that follows seems smaller and easier by comparison than it would if it were the only thing asked.

Door-in-the-face has conditions that matter. It tends to require that the same person make both requests, with little delay between them, and that the second request seem like a genuine concession rather than an unrelated favor. If too much time passes, or if it is obvious the huge first request was never meant to be accepted, the effect weakens. It is worth noticing how differently these two persuasion techniques work: foot-in-the-door relies on the target's shifting self-image after a small free choice, while door-in-the-face relies on social pressure to reciprocate a concession in the moment. Both show that the order and size of a request, not just its content, shapes whether people say yes.
